messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Graphic Designer
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 40

**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 41-year-old married South Asian man who works as a graphic designer for a mid-sized marketing firm. He presents with a guarded posture, his hands folded tightly in his lap, his eyes often fixed on a spot on the floor. He speaks in a low, measured tone, pausing frequently to collect himself.

The event that changed everything happened fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday night. He had been working late on a campaign for a new client, a tech startup. The deadline was the next morning, and he was the only one left in the office, save for the night security guard. He describes the office as a silent, cavernous space, lit only by the glow of his dual monitors and the emergency exit signs. He was focused, his mind pure code and color palettes, when he realized his car—a leased sedan—was parked in a spot that was technically reserved for visitors. It was a minor infraction, something he’d done a dozen times before without issue. But that night, a patrol car had been circling the building.

He saw the police cruiser’s headlights sweep across the glass front doors. He remembers a sudden, cold dread. He didn’t think; he just reacted. He grabbed his messenger bag and walked out to the parking lot. The officer, a large man with a shaved head, was already out of his car, standing by Mr. A.’s driver’s side door. The officer asked for his license and registration. Mr. A. provided them, his hands trembling. The officer then asked him to step out of the car. Mr. A. complied, his heart hammering so hard he could feel it in his throat. The officer then asked him to place his hands on the hood of the car. Mr. A. did so, his mind screaming, *I haven’t done anything wrong*. The officer patted him down. He asked Mr. A. why he was working so late. Mr. A. explained the deadline. The officer asked if he had anything in the car he shouldn’t have. Mr. A. said no. The whole interaction lasted perhaps eight minutes. The officer gave him a warning for the parking violation and told him to move his car. He got back in his cruiser and drove away.

Mr. A. did not move his car. He stood in the parking lot for a long time, his hands still pressed against the cold metal of the hood, his breath coming in shallow gasps. He felt a profound, almost physical shame. He was a professional, a father of two, a man who paid his taxes and never even got a speeding ticket. But in that moment, he had been reduced to a suspect, a potential threat. He remembers the officer’s eyes, flat and unseeing, as if Mr. A. were not a person but a problem to be solved.

Since that night, Mr. A. has not worked late. He leaves the office by 5:30 PM, regardless of deadlines. He has started taking the bus, even though it adds forty minutes to his commute. He cannot explain why, but the thought of sitting alone in his car in the dark, in the parking lot, fills him with a visceral terror. At work, he has become withdrawn. He used to collaborate freely with his team, sketching ideas on whiteboards. Now he communicates almost exclusively through email and Slack. He avoids the firm’s open-plan layout, feeling exposed and watched. His boss has noticed a decline in his creative output. He used to be the one who pitched bold, unconventional concepts. Now he plays it safe, sticking to templates and established designs. He describes it as a “shrinkage” of his imagination.

At home, his wife has grown frustrated. He is irritable, easily startled by the doorbell or a car backfiring. He has stopped driving her to the grocery store on weekends. He has nightmares, not of the officer, but of being trapped in a small, dark room with no windows. He wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart racing. He often lies awake for hours, replaying the eight minutes in the parking lot, trying to find the moment where he could have done something differently, something that would have prevented the shame. He has stopped attending his son’s soccer games, because the loud cheers and the sudden movement of the crowd trigger a feeling of being overwhelmed and unsafe.

He sits in my office, a graphic designer who now designs his life around a single, brief encounter. The world he once navigated with easy confidence has become a landscape of potential threats. He is a man trying to edit the terror out of his own existence, frame by frame.
